description:
We are a team of students and technology enthusiasts who share a common passion for space and innovation. By combining our skills in programming, design, and problem solving, we aim to create meaningful and engaging solutions.

For the Space Mission Design Game challenge, we plan to develop an interactive platform where users can build and manage their own space missions while learning about real-world engineering constraints and scientific objectives.
summary: SOL 14: Red Horizon is a browser game in which students design a crewed Mars mission under real NASA constraints, live with that design for 14 sols on the surface, and end with a Cause-and-Effect Report Card that shows how each engineering choice shaped mission success. On Sol 0 the player balances budget, mass, power, data bandwidth and orbit: rocket and transfer trajectory, landing site, power source, battery, insulation, up to 5 of 9 real NASA instruments and the communication link. On Mars, every one of those choices comes back: the battery decides whether the greenhouse survives the night, the camera decides photo quality, and science only counts once it reaches Earth through limited relay passes. The game turns abstract mission trade-offs into decisions a student can feel, and every number in it is traceable to a NASA source.
details:
What it does. The game follows the three phases of a real mission.

Design (Sol 0). Five console screens: mission objectives (forensics, science or balanced, with NASA-style minimum and full success criteria); 3 launch vehicles × 2 transfer trajectories (Hohmann ~259 days vs. fast ~180 days) inside the 26-month launch window; 3 landing sites; solar or solar + RTG power, battery size and insulation; up to 5 of 9 real NASA instruments (Mastcam-Z, MEDA, SEIS, RAD, RIMFAX, SuperCam/PIXL, MOXIE, Veggie, Ingenuity); UHF relay only or relay + X-band direct-to-Earth; spare repair kits. Live budget, mass, night-energy and data bars react to every choice, and a single-point-of-failure check flags fragile designs before launch.

Operate (Sols 1–14). After a transit in zero-g, the astronaut explores a base-centred map in 0.38 g. Two main objectives: a forensic investigation of lost spacecraft (Opportunity, Spirit, Phoenix, InSight and bonus Beagle 2: collect evidence, diagnose the failure, compare with the real NASA/ESA finding) and six lab experiments (pendulum, free fall, seed germination in perchlorate-washed regolith, water at the triple point, speed of sound, MOXIE day/night output). Around them run crisis cards (dust storm, marsquake and meteor impact, solar particle event, frozen valve, suit leak and more), a power load-shedding panel, a downlink queue limited by relay passes and light delay, and a point-of-no-return oxygen notch on every EVA. The crew's needs (hunger, thirst, fatigue, morale) compete for the same water that also feeds Sabatier fuel production. The player digs for real Mars minerals (hematite "blueberries", an iron-nickel meteorite, gypsum veins, olivine in a lava tube), grows lettuce, radish and zinnia in the greenhouse, exercises like ISS crews, upgrades solar and ISRU systems to level 3, and repairs the Mars Ascent Vehicle with tools and salvaged parts.

Evaluate. The ascent vehicle launches, an anomaly appears on the horizon and its photo downloads line by line until solar conjunction cuts the signal; how much the player sees depends on the camera and bandwidth chosen on Sol 0. The Cause-and-Effect Report Card then traces decisions to outcomes and compares the player's architecture with Perseverance, Opportunity and InSight.

Benefits. Students rarely get to attempt a whole mission. Here every trade-off is visible as a bar, a number or a consequence, and a failed mission still ends with a report card that explains why it failed.

Scientific corrections we made. Our first draft repeated common Mars misconceptions; each correction is now a mechanic: nights fall to about −80 °C (−60 °C is the global average); in 0.6 kPa air the real heat problem is a clogged radiator, not "hot weather"; the largest recorded marsquake is about M4.7, so quakes topple racks rather than throw crew around; return fuel comes from ISRU (Sabatier, electrolysis, MOXIE), not from radioisotopes; crops take weeks, so growth is compressed and labelled; one-way light delay is about 3–22 minutes and solar conjunction blocks contact.

How we built it. Vanilla JavaScript and HTML5 Canvas, no framework or install, hosted on GitHub Pages. One shared game state; every number lives in data/nasa_data.json with its source URL, and values simplified for gameplay are flagged as simplified. All text is bilingual (English/Turkish). Sound effects are synthesized live with the Web Audio API. More than 130 automated tests check formulas, data provenance, translations and full playthroughs by a headless bot.

Fiction notice. The map is compressed, the lava tube is fictional (real candidate skylights are on Tharsis volcanoes such as Arsia Mons), and the UFO scene is fiction, a tribute to the 1976 Viking "Face on Mars" pareidolia episode. All three are labelled in the game.
